title: CTBench: Synthetic Crypto Data That Teaches Trading
one_liner: CTBench is the first benchmark that tests whether synthetic cryptocurrency price data can train models to spot real trading opportunities, not just match statistical patterns.
lead: Cryptocurrency markets never close. Prices swing wildly. Old patterns break suddenly. When researchers want to test trading strategies, they need realistic fake price data for practice. CTBench says: stop testing fake data against fake metrics. Instead, train on synthetic data and see if it actually wins money on real prices.

problem.h2: Old benchmarks measure the wrong thing
paras: Cryptocurrency prices move 24 hours a day, jump violently, and shift mood fast. When you want to test a trading strategy, you need lots of practice data. Real price history is limited. So researchers build fake price generators that copy real prices. But how do you know if the fake data is actually useful?

The old answer: measure how close the fake matches the real. Check if average price, volatility, and correlations are the same. But here is the trap. A fake dataset can look statistically identical to reality and still be useless for trading. A trader cares about one thing: can I use this fake data to train a model that wins money on real prices? Old benchmarks never asked that question.

callout.html: Does training on this synthetic data let a model spot real profit opportunities in real prices?

steps.text: Chop real price history into overlapping train and test windows.
Train a fake-data generator on the training window only.
Feed the fake data to a forecaster to train it.
Run the trained forecaster on real prices in the test window.
Measure accuracy and also simulate actual trading dollars won or lost.

paras: Instead of asking a fake-data generator to match averages and spreads, CTBench asks it to produce data that trains useful trading models.

hidden.h2: Dual-task fidelity: two ways to measure if fake data is worth anything
hidden.name: whether fake data is useful for the real job
paras: A hidden quantity buried in the old approach: nobody agreed on what to measure. CTBench names two. First, Predictive Utility: feed fake data to a model, train it, then test it on real prices. How accurate is the model at forecasting? That measures whether the fake preserves temporal patterns (the rhythm of price movement over time) and cross-sectional patterns (how different tokens move together). Second, Statistical Arbitrage: the old method assumes market prices wander randomly but sometimes snap back like a rubber band stretched and released. CTBench fits the residuals (the parts unexplained by trends) to an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, which models exactly that snapping-back. Then it simulates a trading strategy: whenever the model spots that rubber-band tension, it bets on the snap. Measure the profit. Both scores together reveal the trade-off: can fake data look statistically good AND teach profitable trading, or do those require different choices?

The paper estimates both by running forecasting models and arbitrage backtests on eight different fake-data generators across four distinct market regimes (bull, bear, volatile, stable) on 452 cryptocurrency tokens.

heat.caption: Darker means more critical to spotting real profits. Highlights mark the dual tasks.

reads.html: CTBench measures two separate things: (1) does fake data let a model forecast real prices correctly, and (2) does fake data teach a model to spot and profit from real mean-reversion signals in real markets. These two goals can pull against each other.

The Predictive Utility task trains a TSG model, reconstructs both train and test sets, feeds those to a forecasting model, and evaluates accuracy. The Statistical Arbitrage task fits residuals to an OU process, generates trading signals, and measures total profit, value-at-risk, and expected shortfall.

mechanism.h2: Why splitting the test into two jobs reveals the real trade-off
paras: A fake-data generator faces a dilemma. It can optimize to match the statistical snapshot (mean, variance, correlations) of real data. That looks good on a report. But forecasting models do not care about that snapshot. They care about sequences: what pattern follows this pattern. And arbitrage models care about one thing: places where prices diverged from their average and are about to snap back. These are different targets. A method that chases statistical accuracy might ignore the sequences. A method optimized for profit might distort the correlations. CTBench forces both into the light by running both tests.

Here is why this works: when you train a fake-data generator only on statistical measures, you get a generator that fools those measures but not a trader's brain. When you test it only against forecasting accuracy, you measure something different from profit (you might forecast direction but lose money on timing or risk). By forcing the generator to survive both scrutinies, CTBench exposes the honest game: which generator actually makes fake data that teaches a model to win real trades, not just look smart?

stages.s: Path A: Train forecasting model, test on real prices
Path B: Fit mean-reversion model, backtest trades
Accuracy + Profit metrics reveal the trade-off

math.h2: The mean-reversion signal in one equation
math.words: residual fit to Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process where mean-reverting residuals are used to generate trading signals
math.equation: dr_t = theta * (mu - r_t) * dt + sigma * dW_t
symbols: the residual (price gap) at time t
the speed of reversion (how fast the snap-back happens)
the equilibrium (what the gap wants to return to)
a random jiggle in the price

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a token's price drifts 8 dollars above its average. theta=0.5 means half that gap closes per day.
Starting gap: 8 dollars. After 1 day, expected gap: 0.5 * (0 - 8) = -4 dollars, so gap shrinks to 4.
After 2 days: 0.5 * (0 - 4) = -2, gap shrinks to 2. The rubber band pulls it back.
A trader bets that the gap will close. If it closes faster, the trade wins. If noise dominates (sigma is large), the snap-back is uncertain and the bet loses.

math.note: The equation captures the intuition: when price drifts too far from average, the market pulls it back, but randomness adds uncertainty.

bars.h2: Trade-off: statistical similarity versus trading profit

charts.title: A method optimized for statistical accuracy
charts.note: Chasing statistical measures misses the profit signals.

charts.title: A method optimized for regime-aware generation
charts.note: Respecting market regimes improves both fidelity and actual trades, because a bull market has low volatility and positive momentum while a bear market has high volatility and negative momentum—a generator that learns which regime it is in can produce fake data that matches the real regime, so the trained model sees examples of the behavior it will actually encounter.

items.html: A generator can memorize the exact training prices and reproduce them. It looks statistically perfect and teaches forecasting perfectly. But in a new market regime (the test window), the fake data is useless because it does not contain the new regime.

A generator might match average volatility but fail to reproduce the rare, huge crashes that happen in crypto. A model trained on the fake data thinks risk is low. It gets wiped out in real trading when a crash arrives.
Some methods generate each token independently. In reality, when Bitcoin crashes, most altcoins crash too. A model trained on uncorrelated fake data makes hedging mistakes.

CTBench exposes these by measuring both forecasting accuracy and real profit across different market regimes. A method fails the test if it trades well in the training regime but profits vanish in the test regime, or if tail risks destroy profits even when forecasting looks good.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Pick a cryptocurrency and a market regime (e.g., bull market March-May, bear market June-August). Hold out recent real prices as the test set. Pick two fake-data generators: one optimized for statistical accuracy, one optimized for forecasting on held-out data. Train each generator on the earlier prices. Use each generator to produce synthetic training data. Train a forecasting model on the synthetic data. Backtest on the held-out real prices. Measure: (1) forecast accuracy (e.g., direction prediction, mean absolute error), (2) simulated trading profit over the test window, (3) drawdown (worst cumulative loss). Compare the two generators.
demo.metric_eq: profit_from_synthetic = sum(position_t * return_t) where position comes from a model trained only on fake data
demo.closing: The demo is successful if the winner is the same on both dimensions, or if it honestly shows the trade-off: high accuracy but low profit, or vice versa.
